referred_to_by.content:
This luxurious missal, a kind of manuscript used in Christian church services by a priest and his assistants, was made in the sixteenth century for the bishop of Nola, Antonio Scarampi (1516–76), who lived in what is now Italy. His coat of arms appears at the beginning and end of the manuscript along with his name. The manuscript features masterful decoration executed by the illuminator Fra Vincentius a Fundis (“fra” means “brother” and indicates that Vincentius was a member of a religious order, specifically the Dominicans). His painterly illuminations are representative of a late Renaissance style, called Mannerism, which is characterized by bright colors, animated brushstrokes, exaggerated forms, and flat backgrounds.  

The volume opens with a page with a colorful floral border, and, elsewhere, a full-page image of the Crucifixion is set within an architectural frame made to appear like a marble entablature. The text is arranged in a single column and is augmented by decorated letters, many of which feature either the priest performing the Mass, Christ (both as an infant and as an adult), or chubby winged children called putti. The codex also has musical notation for the sung portions of the Christian Mass. 

This missal attests to the ongoing vibrancy of the manuscript tradition in Nola in the mid-sixteenth century despite the push to print service books so as to ensure their conformity to the reformed standards of Catholic ritual.
